Skip to content
Quiet volume
OverviewSpatial studiesRoom worksheet

Three ways to read a room.

Concept studies for learning and sketching, not built projects or professional construction advice.

The useful threshold

A place to put down a bag and take off shoes changes how an entrance works. Keep this activity out of the main circulation path.

Arrival

Light across a wall

A side-lit surface reveals texture and gives a room depth. Sketch how direct sun moves through the space before committing to a desk position.

Daylight

The quiet edge

Seating feels different when its back is protected and its view is open. Try an existing chair in several positions before buying anything new.

Rest

Draw what is already there

Measure the room, openings, radiators and fixed services. Record dimensions in one unit and keep a separate list of measurements you have not confirmed.

Test with a paper plan

Cut furniture footprints from paper at the same scale as your room. Move them around and preserve a clear walking route. A beautiful arrangement is not useful if a door cannot open.

Know when to ask for help

Do not treat a sketch as permission to change structural walls, ventilation, wiring or fire escape routes. Consult a qualified local professional for any work affecting building safety.

Geometry

Overlap

A circle interrupts a cool plane. Look at which edge appears to sit in front, and how that changes the weight of the whole.

Rhythm

Intervals

Two narrow verticals leave an uneven gap. Imagine moving them closer together and notice how the rhythm changes.

⌞

Space

Quiet corner

An empty corner can be as active as a painted shape. Try following the space around the object rather than the object itself.

●

Colour

Warm field

A warm area advances against a cooler ground. The effect depends on the colour beside it, not just the colour alone.

Counterweight

What does an eyepiece change?

Compare magnification and an approximate true field of view. Actual usable fields depend on the eyepiece and telescope design.

Start with the wider view.

Magnification is telescope focal length divided by eyepiece focal length. A simple field estimate divides the apparent eyepiece field by that magnification.

The estimate ignores field stops and distortion. It is a way to compare setups, not a guarantee of optical quality or useful magnification.

OverviewObserving notesEyepiece calculator

A notebook for after dusk.

Use a current sky chart for your date, location and hemisphere. This site does not fetch weather, position or ephemeris data.

Find the horizon

Choose a safe, permitted observing spot with a clear view and an easy way home. Note trees, buildings and artificial light sources before dark.

Start wide

Learn a few bright stars and large patterns with the unaided eye. Binoculars can be a useful next step, but a stable posture and a simple chart matter more than magnification.

Keep a short log

Record the date, approximate time, conditions and what you actually noticed. A sketch with a few labelled points is often more useful than a long list of targets.

Protect your eyes and equipment

Never point binoculars or a telescope at the Sun without a properly designed and correctly fitted solar observing system and expert guidance. Do not look through an optical finder at the Sun.

A loaf for the day ahead.

Use these notes to choose a style, then follow a complete tested recipe for mixing, proofing and safe baking temperatures.

Everyday tin loaf

A supported dough is an approachable first bake. A little oil softens the crumb; a tin makes shaping forgiving. Weigh ingredients rather than scooping cups of flour.

Country-style round

A freestanding loaf needs enough dough strength to hold its shape. Stretch and fold gently. A supported proofing basket can help, but a floured cloth in a bowl also works.

Flatbread for supper

A small batch of flatbread is useful when you have less time. Keep the dough covered while it rests. Cook a test piece first so you can adjust the thickness and heat.

Keeping bread well

Cool on a rack so steam can escape. Keep a cut loaf wrapped for short storage, or slice and freeze portions. Do not keep a fresh loaf sealed while it is still warm.

OverviewWorkshop notesFit estimate

Keep it rolling.

Use these checks as reminders. Follow the bicycle and component manuals for procedures and torque values.

Air

Read the tyre’s permitted pressure range and use a gauge. Rider weight, tyre width and surface all affect your starting pressure. Inspect for cuts and embedded debris while the wheel turns.

Brakes

Check that each brake engages before its lever reaches the handlebar. Look for worn pads and damaged cables or hoses. Stop riding if braking is unreliable and ask a qualified mechanic.

Chain and contact points

Wipe off grit before adding lubricant. Keep oil away from braking surfaces. Check that the saddle and bars have not moved; use the correct torque procedure rather than tightening by feel.

Choose the route first

A city bicycle prioritises visibility, comfort and practical carrying. A gravel bicycle makes more room for varied surfaces. Neither label replaces a good test ride and properly fitted contact points.

OverviewGame shelfDice tray

Small games you can make.

Original microgame ideas using paper, a pencil and ordinary dice. Agree on the rules before starting; no commercial games are represented.

Search by material or choose a style of play.

2–6

Dice

Race to thirty

Take turns rolling one six-sided die. Add it to your score or roll again. A one loses the points from this turn. Bank before ending a turn. First to 30 wins.

2–4

Cooperative

The shared total

As a group, roll six dice one at a time and choose plus or minus for each result. Aim to finish as close to 12 as possible. Everyone discusses each choice.

2

Paper

Three by three

Draw a 3×3 grid. Alternate writing unused numbers 1–9 in empty cells. Player A scores the top and bottom rows; B scores the left and right columns. Highest total wins.

2–6

Paper

Word ladder

Choose a four-letter starting word. Each player changes one letter to form a different word. No repeats. If a player cannot move, start a new ladder and give the previous player a point.

2–6

Cooperative

Quiet collection

Each person writes three ordinary objects on slips. Draw one and describe it without its name. The group gets one point if someone guesses within one minute.

2–6

Dice

Closest pair

Everyone rolls two dice three times, keeping their lowest difference. Ties use the higher total of that pair. After five rounds, the most round wins takes the game.

A practical server handbook.

An independent guide for Java Edition communities, not an official service or a hosting offer.

Pick one server family

Vanilla keeps the smallest moving parts. Paper-compatible servers add plugin choices; modded worlds need compatible versions on every client. Keep a list of the exact files and versions used.

Distance is a capacity setting

Simulation distance affects the area that keeps ticking. View distance affects chunks sent to players. Lower them before buying more memory, and compare tick time while friends explore in different directions.

A backup is a restore plan

Stop the server or use its supported save procedure before taking a consistent copy. Keep backups away from the world directory. Test a restore into a separate folder before you need it.

Keep the join boundary clear

Leave online-mode enabled, use an allowlist for a private group and keep administrative access separate. The planner generates settings, not a reachable server. Review all settings before deployment.

OverviewSession notesBeat workbench

A session that stays manageable.

A practical home-recording guide. There are no studio bookings or uploaded recordings on this site.

Prepare the room

Turn off avoidable noise sources and listen from the recording position. Soft furnishings can reduce reflections, but they are not a substitute for understanding the room. Move the microphone before reaching for processing.

Keep a clean signal

Set levels with the loudest expected passage and leave headroom. Avoid clipping at the input; turning down a clipped recording later cannot restore the missing waveform.

Name as you go

Name tracks, takes and versions so that tomorrow’s session is understandable. Keep an untouched copy of the original recording and a separate project backup.

Finish one idea

Choose a limited set of sounds and complete a short arrangement. Take breaks at a comfortable listening level. A finished sketch teaches more than a large folder of unnamed loops.

Care that fits into a day.

These are general household reminders, not veterinary advice. Follow your veterinarian’s guidance for your individual animal.

Food and water

Use an appropriate food and a measured amount agreed with your veterinarian or the product guidance. Changes in appetite or drinking deserve attention; a checklist cannot explain their cause.

Movement and rest

Choose play and exercise suited to the animal’s age, health and comfort. Give cats places to hide and climb safely. Let dogs explore at a comfortable pace and rest afterward.

A shared care note

When several people help, keep a clear note of meals, walks and any instructions. Never rely on memory for prescribed medication; follow the veterinarian’s directions exactly.

Notice changes early

A new behaviour, altered movement or a change in eating can be useful information for a veterinarian. Seek professional help for health concerns rather than treating an online routine as a diagnosis.

Start with the light you have, leave room for new growth and get to know a plant before building a jungle.

Read the light, not the room.

Bright, indirect

A luminous spot with no long spell of harsh direct sun. Observe it over a whole day.

Gentle daylight

Near a window but away from the strongest rays. Seasonal light changes matter.

Lower light

Growth slows down. Most plants still need daylight; no plant lives indefinitely in darkness.

A slow-growing, broad-leaf plant for moderate to lower daylight. Let the surface dry before checking the root zone.

Spider plant

Arching leaves suit a shelf near a bright window. Keep the pot draining freely and rotate it for even growth.

Parlour palm

Soft fronds work well in gentle daylight. Avoid standing water, cold drafts and prolonged harsh sun.

Jade plant

A succulent that prefers brighter light and a drying interval. Heavy, wet soil is a more common problem than a missed watering.

Rubber plant

Broad leaves enjoy a bright position. Wipe dust gently and check species-specific pet precautions.

Bird’s nest fern

Read a district slowly.

Fictional places for planning ideas. There are no bookings, live maps or location tracking.

Market lane

Walk the smaller side streets before the main square gets busy. In a real market, check local opening days and ask before photographing people or their work.

Morning

River walk

Leave room for a pause, a water refill and a change in weather. A good route has more than one way to return.

Midday

Reading terrace

Choose a quiet stop with shelter and a clear route back to transport. Check accessibility before building a day around a place.

Afternoon

Plan around one anchor

Choose one activity you care about, then build a generous route around it. Avoid turning every stop into a timed appointment.

Keep a return option

Save the address of your accommodation and your transport details offline. Check current access, public transport and local advice rather than relying on an old screenshot.

Spend with attention

Use local businesses respectfully, keep public spaces clean and make room for the people who use the neighbourhood every day.

About Hosting fieldbook.

A practical hosting fieldbook for static pages and modest projects. Understand the moving parts before choosing a plan.

A useful place to begin

Hosting fieldbook explains the moving parts of a small website: files, HTTPS, updates and a workable recovery plan. It is a learning resource, not a hosting provider.

Using this notebook

The worksheet estimates bytes from explicit assumptions. It does not predict CPU capacity, availability, database latency or a bill. No servers are provisioned and no live systems are probed.

Your privacy

Tools run in this browser. Entries are not uploaded, and the pages load no remote fonts, analytics or advertising. Saved choices and checklist states use this browser’s local storage, scoped to this notebook. Clear site data in your browser to remove them. If storage is unavailable, tools still work and choices last only until the page closes.

Downloads are files created in your browser, not files sent to a service. The hosting server may keep ordinary access logs according to its owner’s settings. No accounts, orders or bookings are accepted here.

Make it your own

The illustrations and learning examples were created for this notebook. Its content is intended to be read, tried and adapted. Begin with the reference pages or open the local tool.

ApproachUseful forWhat you still own
Static hostingDocumentation, portfolios, guidesContent, domain, access to publishing
Managed applicationA small web applicationApplication updates, secrets, data recovery
Virtual serverA project needing system controlOperating system, network policy, all services

Separate publishing from administration

A content change should not need unrestricted server access. Keep deployment credentials scoped to their job and remove unused access.

Know the recovery path

Write down where the files and data live, how a backup is made and how long a restore takes. A backup that has never been restored is an assumption.

Measure the real workload

Traffic and storage estimates help choose a starting point. They do not predict peak concurrency, CPU demand or database latency. Test the actual application before relying on a capacity claim.
